q: What is the fully qualified form of the image reference `postgres:17-alpine`?
explain: Without a registry hostname, Docker uses `docker.io`; official images live in the `library` namespace. The tag defaults to `latest` only when omitted.

q: Production broke after a redeploy although nobody changed the Dockerfile: the base `node:22` now contains a newer Node patch with a regression. What prevents this class of problem?
options: Pinning the base image by digest (e.g. `FROM node:22-bookworm-slim@sha256:...`) and updating it deliberately
explain: Tags are mutable; a digest identifies exact content. Pin digests and update them on purpose (Renovate/Dependabot can automate PRs). `--pull` and `--no-cache` make builds *more* likely to pick up new upstream content.

q:
In this Dockerfile, which instructions re-run after you change only `src/app.ts`?

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
```
explain: The manifests didn't change, so their COPY and `npm ci` stay cached. `COPY . .` includes the changed file, so it and every later step rebuild.

q: Why should `node_modules` be listed in `.dockerignore` for a Node project? (select all)
options: Host-installed native modules may be built for macOS/arm64 and break in a Linux container
Docker cannot copy directories named node_modules
It can make the build context huge and slow
Dependencies should be installed reproducibly inside the build with `npm ci`
explain: Copying host dependencies is non-reproducible and can bring wrong-platform binaries (bcrypt, sharp, esbuild). It also bloats the context. Docker can copy it — that's exactly the problem.

q: An image has `ENTRYPOINT ["node"]` and `CMD ["server.js"]`. What runs with `docker run img --inspect=0.0.0.0 server.js`?
explain: Arguments after the image name replace CMD and are appended to ENTRYPOINT. Only `--entrypoint` replaces the ENTRYPOINT.

q: A Dockerfile ends with `CMD node dist/index.js`. What is the main runtime consequence?
options: The command runs via `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell may be PID 1 and SIGTERM may not reach node, breaking graceful shutdown
The build fails because the command isn't JSON
Environment variables are unavailable to node
The image cannot be run on arm64
explain: Shell form wraps the command in `/bin/sh -c`. Use exec form `CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]` so node receives signals directly, and so the image works without a shell (distroless).

q: Which statements about `ARG` and `ENV` are correct? (select all)
options: An `ARG` declared before `FROM` must be re-declared after `FROM` to be used in that stage's instructions
`ENV` values persist in the image config and are visible at runtime
`ARG` values are not present in the running container's environment
`ARG` is a safe way to pass an npm token because it isn't kept in the image
explain: ARG values used in RUN are recorded in `docker history`, so they are not safe for secrets — use `RUN --mount=type=secret`. Pre-FROM ARGs are only in scope for FROM lines unless re-declared.

q: A colleague's Dockerfile has `RUN apt-get update` on one line and `RUN apt-get install -y libpq5` on the next. Months later, adding another package fails with 404 errors from the Debian mirror. Why?
options: The base image must be re-tagged
The cached `apt-get update` layer holds stale package lists; the new install step uses them
explain: The update step's cache key didn't change, so it was reused with months-old indexes pointing at package versions that no longer exist. Combine update, install and cleanup in a single `RUN`.

q: Your image is 900 MB. `docker history` shows `RUN rm -rf /tmp/build-cache` with size 0B after a 600 MB layer that created that directory. What's the fix?
options: Create and delete the files in the same `RUN` (or produce them in a separate build stage and copy only the result)
Move the `rm` to the top of the Dockerfile
explain: A later layer can only hide files with whiteouts; the bytes stay in the earlier layer. Clean up in the same layer, or use multi-stage builds so the cache never enters the final image.

q: You push `ghcr.io/acme/api:1.2.0` and then tag the same image as `ghcr.io/acme/api:sha-4e1f9c2` and push again. What does the second push upload?
options: All layers again, because the tag is new
Nothing — pushing a second tag is not allowed
Only the manifest reference; all layers already exist in the repository
A compressed copy of the first tag
explain: Registries are content-addressed. Layer blobs with the same digest are already there (`Layer already exists`); the new tag just points at the same manifest.

q: Which `.dockerignore` mistake leaks secrets most often?
explain: `COPY . .` copies everything in the context that isn't ignored. A local `.env` then lives in a layer that anyone with pull access can read. Prefer explicit COPY allow-lists plus a `.dockerignore` safety net.

q: Which tools or commands help you understand what is inside an image and where its size comes from? (select all)
explain: `history` lists layers and sizes, `dive` explores each layer's files and wasted space, `image inspect` shows config and layer digests. `docker port` shows port mappings of a container.

q: What does `docker init` generate for a Node project?
options: A `Dockerfile`, `compose.yaml`, `.dockerignore` and `README.Docker.md`, based on your answers to a few questions
A GitHub Actions workflow that pushes to Docker Hub
explain: `docker init` scaffolds container files using best practices (multi-stage, cache mounts, non-root user). Review and adapt them; it doesn't know your app's dependencies or health endpoints.
